title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array
prompt:
An import bug wrote some of a student's quiz scores twice. The scores are sorted. Write removeDuplicates(nums) that removes the duplicates in place: after the call, the first k slots of nums hold each distinct value once, in the original order, and the function returns k. What is left in the array after slot k doesn't matter. Don't create a new array and don't use splice.

Example: nums = [70, 70, 82, 90, 90, 95] → returns 4, and nums.slice(0, 4) is [70, 82, 90, 95].

Constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 3 × 104; values can be negative; nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

tests.name: small example
quiz scores from the prompt
long runs of duplicates
all the same value
negatives and no-duplicate arrays

hints: "In place" plus "keep some items in order" is the same-direction (read/write) two-pointer shape.
Because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the last value you kept, which is nums[write - 1]. When it's new, copy it to nums[write] and advance write.

Shape:

if (nums.length === 0) return 0;
let write = 1;
for (let read = 1; read < nums.length; read++) {
  if (nums[read] !== nums[write - 1]) {
    nums[write] = nums[read];
    write++;
  }
}
return write;
explain:
Time O(n), extra space O(1). read visits each slot once and nothing ever shifts. The splice version is O(n²) in the worst case because every removal shifts the whole tail of the array.

The same shape solves "move zeros to the end", "remove all copies of a value", and "keep at most two of each" (compare with nums[write - 2]). It's also how compaction works in storage engines: copy the live records forward, then truncate.

In an interview: "I'll use a write pointer for the end of the kept prefix and a read pointer that scans. Sorted means duplicates are adjacent, so I keep a value when it differs from the last kept one. O(n) time, O(1) space."
